title: How to Start Investing in NEPSE: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
excerpt: Want to start investing in the Nepal Stock Exchange? Follow this simple, step-by-step beginner guide covering bank accounts, Demat, Meroshare, broker TMS setup, and your first trade.
body: When I first started exploring the **Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE)**, the biggest hurdle was not picking stocks. It was figuring out how all the different accounts fit together. Between banks, Demat numbers, Meroshare logins, and broker portals, the whole onboarding process can feel confusing if nobody lays it out simply.
If you are ready to move past IPOs and start buying shares in the secondary market, here is the exact step-by-step roadmap to get set up properly in Nepal.
**1. Open a Bank Account With C-ASBA Enabled**
Everything in NEPSE starts with a standard savings account at a commercial or development bank in Nepal.

Once your account is active, ask your bank to activate **C-ASBA** and provide your **CRN (C-ASBA Registration Number)**. You will need this number whenever you apply for Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) or right shares, as it allows the bank to hold your application amount safely until allotment.
**2. Open a Demat Account and Activate Meroshare**

Think of a **Demat account** as a digital locker that holds your shares electronically instead of paper certificates. You can open one through a licensed Depository Participant (DP), usually a bank's merchant banking arm or your stock broker.

At the same time, request **Meroshare** access. Meroshare is the online portal by CDSC where you apply for IPOs, check your portfolio holdings, calculate your Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), and transfer shares after selling them.
**3. Register With a Licensed Stock Broker for TMS**
To buy and sell shares directly in the live secondary market, you need an account with a SEBON-licensed stock broker.

Most brokers now offer online KYC registration. Once verified, they will give you login credentials for your **TMS (Trade Management System)** account, which is the web portal used to place buy and sell orders during market hours from Sunday to Thursday, 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM.
**4. Load Collateral and Place Your First Small Order**
Before buying shares on TMS, you transfer funds from your bank into your broker account as **collateral** (usually via ConnectIPS).
Start with a small amount you are comfortable learning with. Stick to fundamentally sound companies or mutual funds first rather than chasing volatile stocks hitting daily circuits.
**My Take**
From my own experience watching beginners enter NEPSE, getting the accounts opened is easy, *but having patience once your TMS screen turns green or red is the real test*.
Set up your system cleanly, start small while learning how orders and T+2 settlement work, and focus on understanding the businesses you buy rather than following daily market rumors.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always do your own research and consult a licensed financial advisor before investing in the stock market.*

title: How to Apply for an IPO in Nepal: A Complete Beginner's Guide
excerpt: Want to apply for Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) in Nepal? Learn how IPOs work, what documents you need, and how to apply online through Meroshare in minutes.
body: For almost every young investor in Nepal, including myself, applying for an **Initial Public Offering (IPO)** is the very first step into the stock market. Before you ever open a broker account or look at live candlestick charts on NEPSE, an IPO lets you buy shares directly from a company at its base price before it lists on the exchange.
If you are completely new to investing in Nepal and want to start applying for IPOs properly, here is how the process works from start to finish.
**What Is an IPO in Simple Terms?**
When a private company in Nepal wants to raise money from the public to expand its business or pay off loans, it offers its shares to everyday investors for the first time.

In Nepal, most general public IPOs are issued at a par value of **Rs. 100 per share**, with a minimum application of **10 units (Rs. 1,000)** (though some companies issue shares at a premium or via book-building). Because millions of Nepalis apply for limited shares, allotment usually happens through a lottery system. If you get allotted, the shares appear in your account; if not, your bank releases your blocked money automatically.
**What You Need Before Applying**
You do not need a stock broker account to apply for an IPO. You only need three basic things set up through a commercial or development bank:

* **A Savings Bank Account:** An active account with at least Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 2,000 in balance.
* **Demat Account:** A digital locker where your allotted shares are stored safely.
* **Meroshare and CRN:** Online login access to CDSC's **Meroshare** portal, plus your **C-ASBA Registration Number (CRN)** from your bank so funds can be held during the application window.
**How to Apply Online Through Meroshare**
Once an IPO opens (usually for four working days), applying takes less than two minutes:
1. Log in to your **Meroshare** portal or mobile app.
2. Go to the **My ASBA** tab and select **Apply for Issue**.
3. Pick the open company IPO (make sure you select *Ordinary Shares* for the general public, not local or foreign-employment quotas unless eligible).
4. Enter your applied units (usually **10 kitta** for oversubscribed issues), select your bank, type your **CRN**, and confirm with your **4-digit transaction PIN**.
**My Take**
From my own experience starting out in Nepal's market, IPOs are the safest way to build the habit of investing without risking big money.

Do not get discouraged if you miss several allotments in a row because of high applicant numbers. Stay consistent, keep a small balance ready in your bank account, and use that time to learn how companies actually perform once they list on NEPSE.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always verify official IPO announcements through CDSC, SEBON, or Meroshare before applying.*

title: NEPSE vs. Forex: What Trading Both Taught Me About Liquidity
excerpt: Comparing the Nepal Stock Exchange with the global forex market reveals a critical lesson every beginner misses. Learn how liquidity works in both markets and why it changes how you enter and exit trades.
body: Having spent over four years watching the **Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE)** and the past couple of years studying **forex and gold (XAUUSD)**, I often get asked which market is better for a young trader in Nepal.

The truth is, comparing them is not about which one makes more money. Watching both markets side by side taught me one of the most important concepts in trading: **liquidity**, or how easily you can enter and exit a position without moving the price against yourself.
**1. NEPSE Shows You What Happens When Liquidity Dries Up**
In NEPSE, trading runs from 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM Sunday through Thursday, with a strict **10% daily circuit limit** on individual stocks.

When strong news or sector hype hits a low-cap hydropower or microfinance stock, buyers flood the order book. The stock hits a positive circuit within minutes, and suddenly you cannot buy a single share even if you want to. The exact opposite happens when panic hits. Everyone lines up to sell at the negative circuit, and there are zero buyers on the other side. *You are locked in until sentiment shifts.*
**2. Forex Shows You How Price Hunts Liquidity**

Forex operates on a completely different scale. With trillions of dollars moving daily across Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York, you almost never worry about getting stuck in a circuit freeze on major pairs like **EUR/USD** or **XAUUSD**.

Instead, liquidity in forex shapes *where* price moves. Institutional players need large pools of resting orders to fill big positions. That is why you often see price sweep just above an obvious resistance level or below a clean support zone, trigger retail stop losses, and then reverse sharply. In NEPSE, lack of liquidity traps you; in forex, abundance of liquidity hunts your stops.
**3. Timing Matters Differently in Both**

In NEPSE, volume spikes around the opening hour and the final thirty minutes before 3:00 PM, while mid-day often drifts quietly. In forex, trading during the quiet morning hours in Nepal feels slow until European and US volume steps in during the afternoon and evening.
**My Take**
Studying both NEPSE and forex made me realize that a chart pattern means nothing without understanding the liquidity behind it.

Whether you are buying shares in Kathmandu or analyzing gold setups on MetaTrader, always check if there is enough volume to support your trade, and never place your stop loss where the crowd puts theirs.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always do your own research and verify local regulations before participating in any financial market.*

title: What 4 Years of Watching NEPSE Cycles Taught Me About Crowd Psychology
excerpt: After 4+ years of following the Nepal Stock Exchange, one pattern repeats every cycle. Learn how retail crowd psychology drives NEPSE bull runs, panic sell-offs, and how beginners can avoid getting trapped.
body: Over the past four years of watching and participating in the **Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE)**, I have seen full market cycles play out right in front of me. I have watched quiet accumulation phases turn into massive bull runs, and I have watched those same rallies fade into long, frustrating bear markets.

When you first start looking at NEPSE, it is easy to think prices move purely because of company profits, bonus shares, or central bank policies. Those things definitely spark the move, *but crowd psychology is what pushes prices to extremes*.
**1. Everybody Wants to Buy at the Top**
One of the clearest patterns in NEPSE is when retail interest peaks.

During the early stages of a bull market, when quality stocks and mutual funds are trading at reasonable valuations, almost nobody is talking about the market. Volume stays low, and people hesitate because the recent memory of losses is still fresh.

Fast forward six months, after the index has already climbed hundreds of points, and suddenly everyone at tea shops, family gatherings, and on social media is asking which stock to buy. Beginners enter heavily right when early investors are looking to book profits. *By the time a stock feels completely safe to buy, most of the easy upside is already gone.*
**2. Fear Makes People Sell Quality at a Discount**
The exact opposite happens during a bear cycle.

When the market drops week after week and red portfolios take over social media feeds, panic spreads fast. Instead of looking at company fundamentals or long-term value, retail investors sell good stocks at steep losses simply to stop the emotional discomfort of watching their screen turn red every afternoon.
**3. Rumors Move Faster Than Real Data**

In a smaller market like NEPSE, herd behavior gets amplified by unverified tips. Whenever a sector like hydropower or microfinance starts hitting positive circuits, crowds rush in without checking earnings, book values, or floorsheet volume. When sentiment flips, those same stocks hit negative circuits with zero buyers left to exit into.
**My Take**
Watching NEPSE over the last few years taught me that your biggest advantage is simply staying calm while everyone else is reacting emotionally.

You do not need to predict the exact top or bottom of a cycle. Just remember that when everyone around you is overly excited, it is time to manage risk, and when everyone is panicking, it is time to do your homework quietly.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always do your own research and consult a licensed financial advisor before investing in the stock market.*

title: Forex Trading Sessions in Nepal Time (NPT): Best Hours to Trade
excerpt: Wondering when the forex market moves fastest in Nepal? Learn the exact Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York session timings in Nepal Time (NPT) and the best evening overlap hours to trade.
body: When I first started watching forex and gold charts here in Nepal, I made a classic beginner mistake. I would open MetaTrader in the morning, see price barely moving for hours, and force trades out of boredom. Once I understood how global trading sessions line up with **Nepal Time (UTC+5:45)**, everything about market rhythm clicked.
Even though the forex market runs 24 hours a day from Monday to Friday, volume and price movement depend entirely on which major financial center is open.
**The Four Forex Sessions in Nepal Time**
Because Nepal does not observe Daylight Saving Time, our session hours shift by one hour twice a year when the US, UK, and Australia change their clocks. Here is the schedule in **Nepal Time (NPT)**:
**Sydney Session:** 2:45 AM to 11:45 AM NPT (3:45 AM to 12:45 PM from April to October)*. This is the quietest start to the trading day, mostly moving AUD and NZD pairs.
**Tokyo (Asian) Session:** 5:45 AM to 2:45 PM NPT (year-round). Price often consolidates in tight ranges, with better movement on JPY pairs.
**London Session:** 1:45 PM to 10:45 PM NPT (12:45 PM to 9:45 PM from April to October). Volume picks up sharply in the afternoon as European banks enter the market.
**New York Session:** 6:45 PM to 3:45 AM NPT (5:45 PM to 2:45 AM from April to October). Major US economic news and heavy liquidity hit the charts during this window.
**The Best Window for Traders in Nepal**
If you trade major pairs like **EUR/USD, GBP/USD, or gold (XAUUSD)**, the highest volume and cleanest setups happen during the **London and New York overlap**.

In Nepal, that peak window runs from **6:45 PM to 10:45 PM NPT** *(5:45 PM to 9:45 PM in summer)*. Nearly half of all daily forex volume flows through these four hours, giving you tighter spreads and stronger momentum without staying up all night.
**My Take**
From my own experience tracking market structure, knowing *when* not to trade is just as important as knowing your entry setup.

Instead of staring at slow morning charts, focus your screen time around the afternoon London open or the evening London and New York overlap. Trading during high-liquidity hours keeps your routine simple and prevents overtrading in dead markets.
*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always practice proper risk management and verify local regulations before trading.*

title: How Can I Start Forex Trading? A Beginner's Roadmap
excerpt: Want to start forex trading without blowing your first account? Follow this simple, step-by-step beginner roadmap covering market basics, chart setup, demo practice, and risk management.
body: When I first started learning about forex trading a couple of years ago, I felt completely overwhelmed by all the noise online. Every video promised quick profits, every guru had a different strategy, and I had no clear idea what to actually do on day one.

If you are a beginner trying to figure out how to start forex trading properly, ignore the flashy payout screenshots and focus on building a simple, structured routine. Here is the exact step-by-step roadmap I wish I had when I started.
**1. Learn How the Forex Market Actually Moves**

Before looking at complicated indicators, understand the basics of what you are trading. In forex, you trade currency pairs like EUR/USD or commodities like gold (XAUUSD), buying one currency while selling another.

Spend your first week learning core terms like pips, lot sizes, leverage, spread, and liquidity. More importantly, pay attention to trading sessions. The market moves very differently during the quiet Asian session compared to the high-volume London and New York sessions.
**2. Set Up Your Charting and Trading Tools**
You do not need expensive software to start. Set up two free tools that almost every serious trader uses:
**TradingView:** Use this to analyze clean candlestick charts, mark support and resistance levels, and study market structure.
**MetaTrader 4 or MetaTrader 5 (MT4/MT5):** Use this to practice placing demo orders, setting stop losses, and calculating position sizes.
**3. Pick One Pair and One Simple Strategy**
One of the biggest mistakes beginners make is jumping across ten different currency pairs and changing strategies every week.

Pick just one or two active instruments, such as EUR/USD or XAUUSD, and stick to a single rule-based approach. Whether you study basic market structure, price action, or ICT concepts, focus on understanding why price moves from one liquidity zone to another rather than blindly following indicator signals.
**4. Practice on a Free Demo Account With Strict Risk Rules**
Open a free demo account and treat it like real money. For at least two to three months, focus on risk management instead of profit targets.
Never risk more than 0.5% to 1% of your account on a single trade, always use a stop loss, and write down why you entered and exited every position in a simple trading journal.
**My Take**
From my own experience studying charts and watching other beginners start out, the people who survive are never the ones looking for shortcuts.

Treat your first few months in forex like learning any real skill. Keep your charts clean, protect your downside first, and only think about trading real capital or prop firm challenges once your demo results are consistent.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Forex trading carries significant risk, so always practice proper risk management and verify local regulations before risking any capital.*

title: Can You Withdraw Prop Firm Payouts to a Nepali Bank Account?
excerpt: Passed your prop firm challenge? Learn how international USD wire transfers reach your Nepali bank account, what documents banks ask for, and which payout options to avoid.
body: When I first started looking into prop firms here in Nepal, passing the challenge felt like the biggest hurdle. Right after that, though, a much more practical question came up among almost every trader I talked to: "If I actually make a profit, can I withdraw it to my Nepali bank account?"
The short answer is yes. However, because prop firms do not send NPR directly through local wallets, the process works through international bank transfers and you need to handle it cleanly.
**How the Payout Reaches Your Bank**

Most established prop firms do not wire money straight from their own company account. Instead, they pay funded traders as independent contractors through third-party payout platforms like Rise (RiseWorks).

Once your payout is approved and sent to your verified payout account, you link your Nepali commercial bank using your Account Number and your bank's SWIFT/BIC code. From there, you withdraw via an international USD SWIFT wire transfer, which typically takes 2 to 5 business days to convert into NPR and land in your account.

One strict rule: Even though many prop firms offer USDC or USDT payout options, never withdraw via crypto in Nepal. Cryptocurrency transactions and P2P conversions are strictly illegal under Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) rules and can get your bank account frozen. Always stick to direct bank wires.
**What Your Nepali Bank Will Ask For**

Commercial banks in Nepal closely monitor incoming foreign currency under NRB guidelines. When an international wire arrives from abroad, your bank may hold the funds briefly and ask you to declare the source of income.
To make sure the transfer clears without stress, keep a clean folder with three things ready:
*Your Prop Firm Certificate or Contractor Agreement
The Official Payout Invoice
Your Payment Processor Receipt (e.g., from Rise)*
Having clear paperwork showing that the funds are performance-based contractor payouts rather than an unverified foreign transfer helps your bank verify the transaction smoothly.
**My Take**
From watching local traders navigate their first withdrawals, the smoothest payouts always go to people who prepare their banking side before they even request a withdrawal.

Before your first payout, call your bank's remittance or SWIFT department and confirm they accept international wire transfers from your firm's payment processor. Keep your paperwork organized, avoid crypto shortcuts, and treat every payout like legitimate foreign income.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal, tax, or financial advice. Always confirm current foreign exchange and remittance procedures with your commercial bank or Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).*

title: How to Start Prop Firm Trading From Nepal: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Want to start prop firm trading from Nepal without wasting money on failed challenges? Follow this practical step-by-step roadmap covering demo practice, firm selection, and bank payment checks.
body: After understanding what prop firms are and how forex rules work in Nepal, the next logical question I get from beginners is: "How do I actually start?"

When I first started looking into prop firms, I noticed that most beginners jump straight to buying the cheapest challenge they see on Instagram. Almost all of them blow that account within a week because they skipped the preparation phase.
If you want to start prop firm trading from Nepal the right way, follow these four steps in order.
**1. Build Your Process on a Free Demo First**
Before spending a single rupee, open a free demo account on TradingView or MetaTrader and trade as if it were a real prop firm challenge.

Set strict rules for yourself: never risk more than 0.5% to 1% per trade, respect a 4% daily loss limit, and track every setup in a simple journal. If you cannot pass a simulated target on a free demo over two or three months, paying for a real evaluation will only burn your cash.
**2. Research Firms That Accept Nepali Traders**
Not every prop firm accepts residents from Nepal, and policies change frequently.
Before choosing a firm, check three things on their official website:
Country Eligibility: Confirm Nepal is not on their restricted countries list.
Payout Track Record: Stick to established firms with transparent rules and verified payout histories rather than brand-new companies offering unrealistic discounts.
Trading Rules: Check their news-trading restrictions, minimum trading days, and drawdown type (static vs. trailing drawdown).
**3. Verify Payment and Payout Methods With Your Bank**
Most Nepali traders use a commercial bank-issued USD prepaid card (dollar card) to pay evaluation fees. However, some banks block payments to trading-related merchant codes.

Call or visit your bank before attempting checkout to confirm whether paying an online evaluation fee is permitted under current Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) guidelines. At the same time, check how the firm sends profit splits—such as direct bank wire transfers—and keep all challenge agreements and invoices saved for documentation.
**4. Start Small and Focus on Survival**
When you are ready to buy your first evaluation, start with the smallest account size (usually a $5,000 challenge).

Do not try to pass the challenge in two days by over-leveraging gold (XAUUSD). Treat it like a slow, steady process. Passing slowly with clean risk management is far better than failing fast and paying for a reset.
**My Take**

From my own time studying market structure and watching how young traders approach prop firms here, the hardest part is not finding a good entry—it is having the patience to wait before spending money.
Treat your demo phase seriously, double-check every banking step beforehand, and protect your capital first.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or legal advice. Always verify current foreign exchange guidelines with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) or your bank before making international payments.*

title: How Can I Trade Forex Legally From Nepal? Practical Options for Beginners
excerpt: Looking for ways to trade forex legally from Nepal? Learn why funding personal offshore brokers violates NRB rules, and explore the practical, compliant steps beginners can take instead.
body: After sharing posts on forex rules and prop firms, the most common follow-up question I get from young people in Nepal is straightforward: "Okay, so how can I actually trade forex legally from here?"

When I started exploring currency pairs and gold charts a couple of years ago, I had to figure this out the hard way. Because Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) tightly regulates foreign currency outflows, you cannot treat forex in Nepal the same way traders do in countries with open capital accounts.
If you want to learn and participate without putting your bank accounts or legal record at risk, here is how to approach it properly.
**1. Avoid Funding Personal Offshore Brokers**
First, be clear about what not to do. Sending your own money from Nepal to fund a personal retail broker account is restricted under the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act.

Do not use informal channels, peer-to-peer (P2P) crypto transfers, or unverified third-party payment agents to bypass banking restrictions. Even if a broker lets you sign up with a Nepali ID, moving money through unapproved channels creates serious legal and banking trouble.
**2. Start With Free Demo Accounts and Market Study**
You do not need to send a single rupee abroad to learn how forex works.

Opening a free demo account on TradingView or MetaTrader gives you live market prices for EUR/USD, gold (XAUUSD), and major indices without moving any money. Spend your first several months building a tested strategy, journaling trades, and learning risk management. Most beginners lose money simply because they skip this step.
**3. Understand the Prop Firm Path (With Bank Verification)**
If you eventually want to earn from your trading skills without depositing personal capital abroad, proprietary trading firms (prop firms) are the route most Nepali traders look into.

Instead of funding a live account, you pay a small evaluation fee to trade a simulated challenge. Because you are paying for an online evaluation service rather than sending investment capital, many traders explore using a Nepali bank-issued USD prepaid card (dollar card).

However, rules vary by bank. Before paying any fee, ask your issuing bank directly whether payments to that specific platform are permitted under current NRB guidelines. If you ever pass and qualify for a profit split, receive payouts strictly through official banking channels and keep all invoices and agreements documented.
**My Take**
From my own time studying market structure and watching how young traders operate here, patience is your biggest edge.

You do not need to rush into paying for challenges or looking for payment shortcuts just to feel like a real trader. Master your analysis on a free demo first, verify every payment step with your bank, and always keep your process clean and compliant.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Foreign exchange regulations and banking policies can change—always verify current rules with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) or your commercial bank before making international payments.*

title: Is Crypto Trading Legal in Nepal? What Beginners Need to Know
excerpt: Is crypto trading legal in Nepal? Learn why Nepal Rastra Bank bans buying, selling, and holding cryptocurrency, and the real risks beginners face before touching any exchange.
body: Whenever I talk about financial markets with young people here in Nepal, the conversation almost always jumps from NEPSE and forex straight to Bitcoin and USDT. With global exchanges and crypto influencers everywhere online, it is easy for beginners to assume trading digital assets is just another normal way to invest.

Before you ever think about downloading an exchange app or buying your first coin, there is one clear answer you need to know: No, crypto trading is completely illegal in Nepal.   
Unlike forex where prop firms sit in a gray area - cryptocurrency has a strict, total ban across the country.
**What Nepal Rastra Bank Rules Say**
Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), along with the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act and the Muluki Criminal Code, prohibits every activity connected to virtual currencies.

This ban covers far more than just day trading Bitcoin. Under Nepali law, buying, selling, holding, mining, transferring, or promoting any cryptocurrency including USDT, Ethereum, stablecoins, and NFTs is a punishable offense. Even using a VPN to access blocked international exchanges or trading through peer-to-peer (P2P) networks does not make the activity legal.
**Why the Ban Is So Strict**
Many beginners wonder why Nepal blocks crypto when neighboring countries like India allow taxed trading.

The main reasons come down to capital flight and consumer protection. Nepal maintains tight controls over its foreign currency reserves. Because crypto allows money to leave the country outside official banking channels, NRB treats crypto purchases as unauthorized foreign investment. On top of that, local authorities have flagged P2P crypto transfers as the primary payment route for online scams and money laundering.
**The Real Risks for Beginners**

In Nepal, getting caught trading or holding crypto is not just a minor warning. Authorities including the Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police and the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) actively monitor suspicious bank and digital wallet transactions.

Violations can lead to frozen bank accounts, confiscation of assets, heavy fines up to three times the transaction amount, and even imprisonment. Furthermore, if you get scammed on a P2P trade, you have zero legal protection because the transaction itself is illegal.
**My Take**
After spending years following NEPSE and financial markets here, one rule has always kept me safe: never build your financial journey on illegal rails.

While global policy discussions around digital assets continue, private crypto trading remains strictly prohibited in Nepal. If you are a young Nepali looking to grow your money or learn market structure, stick to legal, transparent avenues like studying NEPSE or sharpening your skills on legitimate demo accounts rather than risking your bank accounts and legal record over a P2P transfer.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Always refer to official notices from Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) for the latest financial regulations.*

title: What Are Prop Firms in Forex? A Simple Guide for Beginners
excerpt: Prop firms are companies that give traders access to simulated capital to trade forex in exchange for an evaluation fee. Learn how they work and what it takes to pass.
body: When I first started exploring forex a couple of years ago, I ran into a problem almost every beginner faces: I wanted to learn how to trade properly, but I did not have thousands of dollars sitting around to fund a big account. Around that time, I kept hearing other traders talk about passing challenges and getting funded through proprietary trading firms (prop firms).

In simple terms, prop firms are companies that give traders access to simulated capital to trade forex and gold in exchange for a one-time evaluation fee. To get funded, you have to pass a trading test by hitting a profit target without breaking their risk rules.
**What Type of Company Is a Prop Firm?**
Traditionally, a proprietary trading firm is a financial institution that trades its own money—not client deposits—to make profits from the markets.

However, the online retail prop firms popular today work mostly as fintech and evaluation companies. Unlike regulated brokers where you deposit and trade your own money, prop firms provide a simulated trading environment. Because they do not hold public investor deposits, most are registered as standard technology or commercial companies rather than banks or brokers.
**How the Evaluation Model Works**
Normally, if you trade a $100 personal account and make a solid 10% gain in a month, you only earn $10. It is hard to grow a small account without taking reckless risks.

With a prop firm, you pay a small upfront fee—for example, $50 to $100—to take an evaluation challenge on a $5,000 or $10,000 simulated account. If you pass their test, you get a funded account and keep a share of the profits you make, usually 80% to 90%.
**What You Need to Pass**
Prop firms make money from evaluation fees and by using trading data from their top, consistent traders. To filter out gamblers, almost every firm enforces two strict rules:
Daily Drawdown Limit: The maximum amount you can lose in a single day (usually 4% to 5%).
Maximum Overall Loss: The total amount your account can drop before it is permanently breached (usually 8% to 10%).
If you cross either limit even by a dollar, you fail the challenge and lose your evaluation fee.
**My Take**
From watching local traders and studying market structure myself, I see prop firms as a great opportunity—but a terrible shortcut.

If you cannot stay profitable and control your emotions on a free demo account yet, paying for a prop firm challenge will only cost you money. Master your risk management first, treat the evaluation like real capital, and only pay the fee when your strategy is already consistent.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. Always research a firm's background, payout track record, and local payment eligibility before purchasing any trading evaluation.*

title: Is Forex Trading Legal in Nepal? What About Prop Firms?
excerpt: Is forex trading legal in Nepal? Here is the practical difference between funding an offshore broker and using a prop firm under Nepal Rastra Bank rules.
body: Over the past couple of years of following forex and watching the local trading community grow, I have noticed the same pattern everywhere. Young people across Nepal are diving into MetaTrader charts, tracking gold setups, and sharing funded payout screenshots.
Yet almost every beginner I talk to gets stuck on the exact same question before placing their first real trade: Is forex trading actually legal in Nepal?
The honest answer depends on how you enter the market and how money moves across borders.
**Offshore Forex Brokers**
If you live in Nepal and want to deposit your own savings into an international forex broker, you run directly into Nepal's foreign exchange laws.

Under the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act and Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) directives, sending money abroad for speculative margin trading is restricted. A common mistake I see beginners make is assuming a broker is legal locally just because the platform accepts a Nepali citizenship card or passport.

Offshore brokers follow their own country's rules, not Nepal's. Using informal workarounds, third-party wallets, or peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers to fund a foreign trading account carries serious legal and banking risks.
**What About Prop Firms?**
This is why proprietary trading firms (prop firms) have gained so much attention among Nepali traders.

Instead of depositing your own savings as live trading capital, you pay a one-time fee to take an evaluation challenge on a simulated account. If you pass their profit targets without breaking their drawdown rules, you qualify for a funded account and earn a split of the profits.

From a beginner's perspective, the appeal is easy to understand: you are not putting thousands of dollars of personal savings at risk. Your financial exposure is capped at the challenge fee. Still, you can lose that fee, and passing an evaluation or receiving a payout is never guaranteed.
**Can You Pay With a Nepali Dollar Card?**
Nepali banks issue USD prepaid cards (commonly called dollar cards) for approved international online payments. However, having a dollar card does not mean every foreign payment is allowed.

Many banks block payments to trading or high-risk platforms. Before paying any evaluation fee, ask your bank directly if that payment is permitted under current NRB rules. And if you ever receive a payout, keep clear records and use official banking channels.
**My Take**

When I first started learning about forex and market structure, I realized quickly that knowing how to read a chart is only half the picture. Understanding the rules around how you fund and withdraw is just as important.

Prop firms offer a realistic way to test your trading discipline without risking large personal savings. Still, don't let social media hype rush you into buying a challenge. Check the firm's Nepal eligibility, confirm payment rules with your bank first, and understand the full setup before spending a single rupee.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only, not legal or financial advice. Always verify current foreign exchange rules with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) or your bank before making international payments.*

title: Why creativity becomes truly valuable only when backed by strategy?
excerpt: Making things look good is only half the work. True creative impact comes from understanding why a brand exists, who it serves, and the business problem it solves.
body: In graphic design and branding, it is easy to get caught up in aesthetic trends, colors, and typography. But over time, working across both creative design and business development, I realized that aesthetics without strategy rarely produce lasting business value.

Good design catches attention, but strategic positioning builds trust. Before sketching a logo or planning a website layout, you have to ask the fundamental commercial questions: What specific problem are we solving? What expectation are we setting in the client's mind? And can the business consistently deliver on that expectation?

When creativity is anchored to a clear business objective, design stops being a decorative expense and becomes a powerful commercial asset. It communicates value before a word is read and removes friction for the decision-maker.

title: What international client outreach taught me about business development?
excerpt: Notes from lead generation and client communication. Why listening and understanding client requirements beats high-pressure pitches.
body: Stepping into business development, I was tasked with international outreach, lead generation, and digital positioning. Coming in with a design and IT background, I initially wondered how much persuasion would be required.

What I quickly discovered was that effective business development is not about aggressive selling. It is about careful research, active listening, and diagnosing what a prospective partner actually needs before proposing a digital solution.

When you take the time to understand a client's workflows, target audience, and current bottlenecks, the commercial proposal almost writes itself. Genuine communication and clear expectations build partnerships that last.

title: What educating others on financial markets taught me about risk and patience?
excerpt: Observing the stock and forex markets rewards emotional discipline over impulse. Teaching financial literacy showed me how human psychology drives decision-making.
body: When I first started sharing simple posts and answering questions about NEPSE and forex for young people here in Nepal, I thought I was just helping beginners understand the basics. What I did not expect was how much explaining those concepts would reshape my own habits in the market.

You never truly test your understanding of a topic until someone asks you to explain it without charts, jargon, or complicated indicators. Doing that forced me to confront my own blind spots around risk and patience.
**1. Most People Do Not Lose Because of Bad Entries**
When beginners reach out to me, they almost always ask for the same things: a better entry setup, a hidden indicator, or which stock will move next week.

After looking at dozens of beginner questions and blown demo accounts, a clear pattern stood out. Very few people lose money because they cannot spot a trend. They lose because they risk way too much on a single idea. Explaining why risking 1% per trade matters made me much stricter with my own position sizing. When you teach someone else to protect their downside first, you feel foolish ignoring your own stop loss.
**2. Impatience Is Usually Just Boredom in Disguise**

In both NEPSE and forex, the market spends most of its time doing nothing exciting. For months in NEPSE, indices move sideways while liquidity dries up. In forex, price sits in tight ranges before London or New York volume steps in.

Writing about market cycles and liquidity taught me that forcing trades during quiet periods is just paying for entertainment. Seeing beginners rush into prop firm challenges or chase green candles in NEPSE reminded me how expensive impatience really is. Waiting for clear confirmation is not missing out; it is part of the job.
**3. Simplicity Beats Complexity Every Time**
If you cannot explain why you are taking a trade or buying a stock in two simple sentences, you probably do not have a real plan.

Breaking down market structure and basic company fundamentals for others stripped away the unnecessary noise from my own charts. Good risk management and a clear thesis will always beat ten overlapping indicators.
**My Take**
Sharing what I have learned over the past few years of following NEPSE and forex has been one of the best filters for my own discipline.

Teaching keeps you honest. It reminds you every single day that surviving in financial markets has very little to do with predicting the future, and everything to do with managing your risk and having the patience to wait for your setup.

*Disclaimer: This article is for educational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Always do your own research and manage your risk carefully before participating in any financial market.*

title: How an IT background in cybersecurity shapes business thinking?
excerpt: Studying Computer Science and networking gave me a framework for diagnosing friction and understanding how systems behave under pressure.
body: Completing my Bachelor's in Computer Science and IT with a focus on networking and cybersecurity gave me a foundational appreciation for how interconnected systems function and where they break.

In cybersecurity, you learn that vulnerabilities rarely appear in the center of a well-trodden process; they emerge at the handoffs, the edge cases, and the gaps where communication breaks down. The exact same rule applies to business operations and sales funnels.

When a business struggles to convert leads or scale its brand, the bottleneck is almost always an unaddressed operational edge case. Having an IT mindset allows me to analyze commercial problems with structured logic, ensuring that marketing promises align with operational capability.
